hops.afterHeading: The idea: three steps, and a drug changes mainly one
hops.title: The Calabar bean in a surgeon's own eye
hops.text: On January 17, 1863, the Edinburgh eye surgeon Douglas Argyll Robertson put a drop of extract from the Calabar bean, a West African poison, into his own left eye. Twenty minutes later that pupil was half the width of his right. The bean's alkaloid, physostigmine, inhibits acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine lingers at the iris and keeps the pupil small. Atropine acts at a different step: it sits in the muscarinic receptor without activating it. Argyll Robertson showed that atropine opposes the bean, and physostigmine went on to become the first effective glaucoma medication.

hops.title: Ivermectin, golf-course soil and glutamate as a brake
hops.text: In your brain, glutamate mostly excites. In roundworms, glutamate also opens chloride channels that dampen neuron excitability, so at those channels the same molecule works as a brake. In the 1970s the microbiologist Satoshi Ōmura isolated a bacterium, Streptomyces avermitilis, from soil near a golf course in Ito, Japan. Its avermectin, modified into ivermectin, binds the worm channels in their membrane-spanning region and holds them open. Chloride flows in and the worms' nerve and muscle cells go quiet. The young worms behind river blindness are disabled, and the evidence suggests the patient's immune system then clears them. That scoop of golf-course soil earned a share of the 2015 Nobel Prize.

hops.afterHeading: How much: occupancy and the factor 1 + L/K
hops.title: Coffee does not give your brain energy
hops.text: Coffee feels like fuel, but caffeine supplies no energy at all. It is an adenosine receptor antagonist: it sits in brain receptors for adenosine, a chemical cue for sleepiness, without activating them. In 2012, researchers used PET scans in 15 volunteers to estimate how many brain A1 adenosine receptors caffeine fills. Their fitted curve put half occupancy at about 67 micromolar caffeine in plasma, and they concluded that steady coffee drinking through a day might fill up to half of these receptors. In the lesson's competitive model, caffeine sitting at its KB would make adenosine need twice its usual concentration for the same receptor response.

sources.citation: Elmenhorst D, Meyer PT, Matusch A, Winz OH, Bauer A. Caffeine occupancy of human cerebral A1 adenosine receptors: in vivo quantification with 18F-CPFPX and PET. J Nucl Med. 2012;53(11):1723-1729.

audio.title: Three surprises that mapped the synapse
audio.transcript:
Drugs that change brain chemistry look like precision engineering on a textbook diagram. Some of the best known ones stumbled out of a cluttered lab bench, a handful of soil and a hospital ward. Here are three true stories in which a surprise exposed one of the synapse's rules.

First, some leftover crystals. In the mid nineteen fifties, the chemist Leo Sternbach made forty new compounds, hoping to find a better tranquilizer. None of them showed the sedative or relaxant effects he was after, and the results were disappointing. More than a year later, his colleague Earl Reeder drew attention to two crystalline products left over from that work. Testing them turned up a compound with an unexpected ring structure: the first benzodiazepine, chlordiazepoxide. In animal tests it had a pronounced taming effect on monkeys. In nineteen sixty it reached pharmacies as Librium, and diazepam, three to ten times as potent, followed. Both are positive allosteric modulators at G A B A A receptors. On their own they open few or no channels. Their main action is to help the brain's own G A B A open the channel more effectively.

Second, a scoop of soil from a Japanese golf course. You know glutamate as the brain's main excitatory transmitter, but the lesson's rule is that the receptor and the ion gradient decide the sign. In roundworms, glutamate also opens chloride channels, and at those channels the same molecule acts as a brake rather than an accelerator. In the nineteen seventies, the microbiologist Satoshi Omura collected soil near a golf course in Ito, Japan, and isolated a bacterium called Streptomyces avermitilis, still the only natural source of the avermectins. William Campbell found the antiparasitic activity in Omura's culture, and he and his colleagues turned its product, avermectin, into ivermectin, a medicine used against river blindness. Campbell and Omura shared half of the two thousand fifteen Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Ivermectin acts on those worm chloride channels from within the membrane as an allosteric agonist and holds them open. The worms' nerve and muscle cells go quiet. The young parasites are disabled, and the evidence suggests the patient's own immune system then clears them.

Third, a tuberculosis ward on Staten Island. In nineteen fifty-two, physicians at Sea View Hospital were testing a tuberculosis drug called iproniazid. What caught the staff's attention was a side effect: patients showed a striking rise in vitality, became more social, and even asked to leave the hospital. That same year, the biochemist Ernst Zeller showed that iproniazid blocks monoamine oxidase, an enzyme that breaks down amine transmitters. After the psychiatrist Nathan Kline presented it for depression in nineteen fifty-seven, an estimated four hundred thousand patients had taken it within a year. Results from iproniazid, together with other drugs such as imipramine, led researchers to propose the first monoamine hypotheses of depression. That is the lesson's closing point in miniature. Knowing which step of a synapse a drug changes tells you a great deal about the drug, and it still leaves open what caused the illness in the first place.
